catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology and Morphophonology, §2.4 Suprasegmental Phonology, §2.4.1 Stress, pp. 91-94 (chapter-2 pp. 66-69; saved text); fn 44 p. 92; minimal pairs (2.86)-(2.87) p. 94; §2.4.2 Intonation p. 96 (simple perfective verbs, initial stress); fn 19 p. 41 (stressed final short vowels).
catalog_quote: As most previous studies show Gedeo is a stress language (cf. Hudson 1981; Hudson 2007; Wedekind 1985; Wedekind 1990; Mous 2012: 351, among others). Stress in Gedeo is related to morphological classes and also shows contrast, to some extent, at a lexical level (see (2.86) below). The stress falls on the ultimate syllable of the citation form of a word if it is accented, but on the penultimate if the final syllable is not accented. When suffixes are attached to the citation forms, the accent shifts to the penultimate syllable, so the penultimate syllable is stressed. ... However, in the word ɡiirá ‘fire’ (Figure 2.4) it is indicated that the high pitch (236.98 Hz) and greater intensity (88.42 dB) falls on the non-heavy syllable rá than on the heavy syllable ɡii. ... The nouns in (2.85) below carry long vowels with greater intensity, but in all the cases the stress falls on the last syllable, that is, on the non-heavy syllable, which has a high pitch. ... Stress in Gedeo has a contrastive feature. The examples in (2.86) and (2.87) below show the contrast between words that have meaning differences due to stress. (2.86) (a) waadaté ‘a small container made of clay pot’ (b) wáadate ‘He became anxious’ (2.87) (a) ɡandé ‘a name of a disease (of animals)’ (b) ɡánde ‘She hit’

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (74 pp., text, Nitro PDF) and its. The quoted passage is at dissertation p. 91 = PDF page 66 of the chapter-2 file, under the heading 'Stress' (§2.4.1 per the contents file, p. 91; Intonation §2.4.2 p. 95), and matches the report word for word including the citation string '(cf. Hudson 1981; Hudson 2007; Wedekind 1985; Wedekind 1990; Mous 2012: 351, among others)'. Read pp. 91-97 (pp. 66-72) myself: p. 92 shows pitch/intensity, not duration, mark the accent (giirá: high pitch and intensity on the short final -rá, heavy gii- lowest pitch); (2.85) lists six nouns with long penult vowels all stressed on the short final syllable; footnote 44 (p. 92) reads 'On the basis of this one may cl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penult; a lexically accented final syllable takes the stress instead (citation forms such as gogá 'skin', giirá 'fire', waadaté 'pot'). Suffixed forms re-stress the penult. Stress is contrastive: waadaté 'clay pot' vs wáadate 'he became anxious', gandé 'animal disease' vs gánde 'she hit' (the verb members are simple-perfective verbs, which take initial stress, p. 96). Acoustic correlates are higher pitch and greater intensity, not duration (a heavy syllable such as gii- in giirá is unstressed); footnote 44 (p. 92) says one may claim Gedeo is a pitch accent rather than a stress-accent language. Hudson 1989: 6 (comparative HEC dictionary) frames the same pattern by weight: stress on word-final long vowels and diphthongs, otherwise on the penult, with final-stressed short vowels possibly being phonemically long.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphological classes: simple perfective verbs in declarative sentences carry stress on the initial syllable (2.88b-2.91b, p. 96); yes/no questions put a rising intonation on the final syllable (or on a closed penult with 2SG perfective / 1SG imperfective suffixes), pp. 95-97. Footnote 19 (p. 41): words ending in stressed short vowels (kó 'you!', té 'you!') sound long but are short vowels with high pitch; Wedekind 1980b/1990 called this 'underlying vowel length'. Devoicing affects word-final unstressed vowels (pp. 41-43).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, stated for citation forms and for suffixed word forms; intonation treated separately at sentence level (§2.4.2). Acoustic figures 2.2-2.6 (pitch/intensity of single words) support the statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Eyob 2015 describes Gedeo as spoken in the Gedeo Zone (SNNPR, Ethiopia), no dialect distinction made; the older names Darasa/Derasa used by Moreno, Wedekind and Hudson refer to the same language (gede1246). Hudson 1989's stress rule is a blanket statement for all five Highland East Cushitic languages, not Gedeo-specific.

sources.note: §2.4.1 Stress pp. 91-94: stress language; final syllable stressed if accented, otherwise penult; suffixation shifts stress to penult; contrastive (waadaté vs wáadate); correlates pitch + intensity, not duration; fn 44 suggests pitch accent; simple perfective verbs initial-stressed (p. 96).

sources.citation: Hudson, Grover. 1989. Highland East Cushitic Dictionary (Kuschitische Sprachstudien 7). Hamburg: Buske.
sources.note: Introduction, 'Word stress', p. 6: 'In all five HEC languages there appears to be a general rule of stress on word-final long vowels and (rarely) diphthongs, and stress on the vowel of the next-to-last syllable when there is no word-final long vowel or diphthong'; stress marked in entries only where this rule is violated, e.g. on word-final short vowels, which may be phonemically long. Comparative, not Gedeo-specific.
